| Condition | Code |
|---|---|
| key not in the definition table | `unknown_setting` with suggestions |
| key not a process option | `unsupported_scope` |
| readable key outside the allowlist | `unsupported_setting_mutation` |
| parse failure, bound violation, or layer height outside the printer's range | `invalid_setting_value` with `allowed` or bounds |
| spiral-mode conflict or a validator message on a touched key | `incompatible_settings` with the conflicting keys |
| session or revision mismatch, or a before value moved since preview | `stale_workspace` with expected and current |
| user rejected in JusPrin | `approval_rejected` |
| client cancelled or the app closed | `cancelled` |
| no FFF project or no process preset | `workspace_unavailable` |
| the batch call failed after validation | `execution_failed` |
| malformed arguments | `invalid_arguments` |

code and mutates nothing. Never convert an invariant failure into success.

  `Plater::on_config_change`, which invalidates slicing as a sidebar edit

  call `wxGetApp().get_tab(Preset::TYPE_PRINT)->load_config(diff)`.

  key; Orca throws for unknown keys and unparseable values. Canonical value is
  `option->serialize()` after parsing.

  messages for untouched keys are warnings, because the preset was already
  invalid. `Print::validate` is a slicing-time check and is not part of
  preview, as in Orca's own UI.

  `prints.get_edited_preset().name`. The Tab's per-option revert buttons read
  the same data, so they keep working after a tool apply.

77:8. **Search and read cover every process-setting definition; mutation starts with a reviewed allowlist:** `layer_height`, `wall_loops`, `sparse_infill_density`, `sparse_infill_pattern`, `top_shell_layers`, `bottom_shell_layers`, and `brim_width`. Every search and read record says whether the key is writable. Other keys return `unsupported_setting_mutation`. Expand the list only after the real-adapter tests cover the option type, dependency behavior, and visible UI update for each new key.
78-9. **A batch applies whole or not at all, through one current Orca owner.** Never mutate the config behind the visible preset UI and imitate the notifications.
79-10. **Process preset edits are not in project Undo.** Results say so and return previous values so a caller can propose the inverse. No separate settings undo model.
80-11. **A preview that finds invalid settings is a successful call with `valid: false`.** Malformed input is a tool error.
81-12. **All values cross JSON as strings in their canonical Orca serialization.** Callers may send numbers or booleans; the decoder converts them before parsing. All Orca ids cross JSON as strings.
82-13. **Output is bounded and every tool has an output schema.** Results carry both `structuredContent` and the same JSON in one text block.
83-14. **Security posture is unchanged.** No token, loopback only, Origin validated, mutations approved in JusPrin. Nothing in this slice adds remote access.
--
87-### Source model for every value
88-
89:Each returned value states the active process preset name, the current canonical value, whether the key differs from the selected preset, whether it differs from the system parent, and the workspace session id and revision at read time. Do not claim full printer, filament, project, or object inheritance; the contract cannot prove it yet.
90-
91-### Bounded read contracts
92-
93-- `settings_search`: default 10 and maximum 25 matches, deterministic order, optional cursor.
94-- `settings_get`: at most 32 keys per call.
95-- `settings_preview_patch` and `settings_apply_patch`: at most 32 keys per patch.
--
117-|---|---|
118-| key not in the definition table | `unknown_setting` with suggestions |
119:| key not a process option | `unsupported_scope` |
120-| readable key outside the allowlist, on apply or as a preview issue | `unsupported_setting_mutation` |
121:| parse failure, bound violation, or layer height outside the printer's range | `invalid_setting_value` with `allowed` or bounds |
122-| spiral-mode conflict or a validator message on a touched key | `incompatible_settings` with the conflicting keys |
123-| session or revision mismatch, or a before value moved since preview | `stale_workspace` with expected and current |
124-| user rejected in JusPrin | `approval_rejected` |
125-| client cancelled or the app closed | `cancelled` |
126-| no FFF project or no process preset | `workspace_unavailable` |
127-| the batch call failed after validation | `execution_failed` |
--
146-| Rule in Orca | Reached by | Effect | Preview must |
147-|---|---|---|---|
148:| `layer_height` at or below epsilon | `layer_height` | modal warning, reset to 0.2 | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the minimum |
149:| `layer_height` above the printer preset's `max_layer_height` when that is greater than 0.2 | `layer_height` | modal warning, clamp | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the printer's maximum |
150:| `seam_slope_type` is not `None` and the absolute `seam_slope_start_height` is at or above `layer_height` | lowering `layer_height` | modal warning, `seam_slope_start_height` reset to 0 | refuse with `incompatible_settings` naming `seam_slope_type` and `seam_slope_start_height`; evaluate percent values through Orca too; 100% or above also trips this |
151:| `spiral_mode` on and not all of `wall_loops` 1, `top_shell_layers` 0, `sparse_infill_density` 0 | `wall_loops`, `top_shell_layers`, `sparse_infill_density` | yes/no dialog, several keys rewritten either way | refuse with `incompatible_settings` naming `spiral_mode` |
152-| Support-gap rounding block under `#if 0` | none in this build | inactive; `support_top_z_distance` is not rewritten | do not predict or apply a nonexistent change; verify the value stays unchanged |
153-| `sparse_infill_pattern` set to a pattern without multiline support while `fill_multiline` is above 1, in `toggle_print_fff_options` | `sparse_infill_pattern` | silent: `fill_multiline` reset to 1 | predict and report as `normalized_dependency`; apply lists it under `normalized` |
154-
155:Two rules follow from this table. First, the preview evaluates the same rule set against the post-batch clone, using the printer preset and filament count the real adapter can read, so a rule that fires because of a pre-existing value is reported too. Second, dialog rules are blocking issues and silent rules are warnings that name the dependent key and its predicted value. The real-adapter test asserts that no top-level dialog appears during apply for any allowlisted key under every condition in the table, and that every silent rewrite the preview predicted appears in the result's `normalized` list with the actual value.
156-
157-The table is the current audit, not a guarantee. Phase 1 re-reads both functions for every key they read, adds any rule an allowlisted key can reach, and records the audit in the pull request. A rule found later that a tool can trigger is a defect in the preview, not accepted behavior.
158-
159-### Implementation audit against the current checkout
160-
161-The Phase 1 source audit corrected three assumptions in the table above:
--
163-- The support-gap rounding block is inside `#if 0` in `ConfigManipulation.cpp`. The implementation and fake use the active multiline reset as their silent-normalization fixture; they do not invent a support-gap change. The support-gap value remains unchanged.
164-- A percent scarf start height can trigger the dialog at 100% or above. Preview uses Orca's `get_abs_value` for both absolute and percent values.
165:- Every active dialog predicate must be checked, including pre-existing invalid ironing spacing, first-layer height, XY compensation, elephant-foot compensation, alternate-extra-wall settings, infill-lock depth, and fuzzy-skin settings. Spiral mode also checks support, enforced support layers, thin walls, overhang reversal, timelapse, and wrapping detection.
166-
167-After these predicates pass, preview invokes Orca's `ConfigManipulation` on its cloned config with no presentation callbacks. This reuses the authoritative silent-normalization rules, including multiline support, instead of copying their option tables. `TabPrint::update` skips option toggles when there is no active process page or the Dependencies page is active; prediction follows that condition using the public field/page lookup.
168-
169-Live in-app verification also exposed a stateless OpenAI continuation defect: after the first tool call, the adapter discarded the original user request, workspace context, and earlier tool results. A regression reproduced a three-item continuation where five items were required. The adapter now retains the complete turn input and appends each response and tool result, while dispatching only the newest response's tool calls. This is shared conversation transport behavior, not a second settings implementation.
170-
171-Real-adapter verification has demonstrated a successful batch before explicitly opening the process settings page, a single coalesced `Settings` event and revision, unchanged project Undo availability, native field updates and preset revert, inverse patches, stale confirmed values, and no modal calls in the tested cases. Runtime proof and the full completion gate remain required below.
--
262-1. **search**: iterate `Preset::print_options()`, look up each in `print_config_def`, rank deterministically by exact key, key prefix, label substring, then description substring, tie-break by key, page with an opaque `offset:N` cursor, default 10, maximum 25.
263-2. **read**: for each key, definition plus current value from the edited preset, `differs_from_preset` and `differs_from_system` from the dirty accessors, and `writable` from the allowlist. Unknown keys are returned separately with suggestions.
264:3. **preview**: the pipeline in the order given under "Validation and metadata entry points", then every rule in the Hazard 1 table evaluated against the post-batch clone with the printer preset and filament count read from the preset bundle, then `Slic3r::validate`, then the diff. Keys whose parsed value equals the current value are dropped from `changes` and reported as unchanged in `warnings`. No Orca state changes and no event is published.
265-4. **apply**: wrap in `ProjectStateTransaction` so nested notifications coalesce into one event. Re-run preview against the current config. If any before value differs from `confirmed`, return `StaleSettings`; if any blocking issue exists, return `InvalidSettings`; neither mutates. Otherwise build the diff config and call `Tab::load_config`. Read back every touched key and every dependent key the preview predicted, fill `applied`, and return success. The transaction commits one `Settings` change with one new revision.
266-
267-### Registry entries
268-
269-All four are exposed `InApp | Mcp`, availability `Always`, with handlers `SettingsSearch`, `SettingsGet`, `SettingsPreviewPatch`, `SettingsApplyPatch`. The first three are `ReadOnly`; the last is a mutation requiring approval.
270-
--
327-
328-- Search bounds, deterministic order, and cursor paging; an invalid cursor is `invalid_arguments`.
329:- Unknown key suggestions; unsupported scope.
330-- Type, enum, and range errors with the allowed values or bounds in the issue.
331-- The spiral-mode conflict produces `incompatible_settings`; the multiline reset produces a `normalized_dependency` warning in preview and a `normalized` entry with the actual value after apply. Support-gap rounding remains inactive.
332-- Preview mutates nothing and publishes no event.
333-- Apply is atomic: one revision, one `Settings` event, all keys or none.
334-- Apply with a confirmed set whose before value no longer matches returns `StaleSettings` and mutates nothing.
335-- A key equal to its current value is reported unchanged; an all-unchanged patch returns `NoChange`.
--
354-- Applied values appear in the process tab fields and the sidebar dirty indicator.
355-- A sliced plate reports `sliced: false` after apply.
356:- No top-level dialog appears during apply for any allowlisted key under every condition in the Hazard 1 table: layer height at zero, at and above the printer's maximum, lowered below an absolute scarf-seam start height, wall loops or top layers or infill density on a spiral-mode preset, and an infill pattern change on a multiline preset.
357-- The multiline reset is predicted by preview and reported under `normalized` with the actual value after apply. The compiled-out support-gap rounding leaves its value unchanged.
358-- An approved inverse patch restores the pre-batch values.
359-- Orca's preset revert control clears the dirty state after a tool apply.
360-- Project Undo availability is unchanged by an apply.
361-- A GUI edit between preview and apply produces `stale_workspace`.
362-- A GUI edit publishes `Settings` with one new revision.

372-```text
373-open JusPrin with a sliced two-object project
374:→ search "infill", read layer_height and sparse_infill_density
375-→ preview a two-key patch, receive valid with before and after
376-→ apply, reject in JusPrin, values unchanged

429:- Printer, filament, plate, object, or modifier settings.
430-- Expanding the write allowlist beyond the seven keys without the real-adapter coverage decision 8 requires.
431-- Preset switching, saving, or creating presets.

434-- Rendering before-and-after diffs in the Agent page. The existing card is sufficient for v1.

content.text:
The restriction to process settings was a staging decision, not a product rule. The settings tools shipped on 2026-09-04 as a first, narrow slice, and the design says every other kind of settings stays out until it has been built and tested as its own capability. Nothing I found argues that the assistant should never touch printer settings, and the planned tool list already expects a `scope` field for them.

## Where it is written down

**1. The original design doc.** `agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-settings-tools-handoff.md` was added in commit `77c0c6a3c4` (2026-09-04, "Add approved process-settings tools to the shared Agent registry") and removed in `62c0606a09`. Its rule 6 says only the active process preset is in scope, with "No `scope` field, no printer, filament, plate, object, or modifier layers until each is a separately tested capability." Its "Explicit non-goals" list starts with "Printer, filament, plate, object, or modifier settings." It also says a value's reported origin must not claim printer or filament inheritance, because "the contract cannot prove it yet."

**2. The current tool guide.** `62c0606a09` (2026-09-08) moved the lasting parts of that doc into [mcp-tool-extension-guide.md](agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md), under "Process-settings tools: contract and hazards". Standing decision 2 keeps the same wording: no printer, filament, plate, part, or modifier layer until each is a separately tested capability. The only change since then is `target: {objectId}`, added in `c35dcfcd20` (2026-09-16).

**3. The general rule behind it.** "Choose the narrowest honest scope" in the same guide says:

> Never put an enum value such as `printer | filament | process | object` in a schema unless every advertised value works in the fake and real adapter and has the documented inheritance behavior.

So the assistant was never given a choice it could not act on.

## Why "separately tested" is real work

The reasons are recorded in both docs:

- **Settings changes go through the settings page's own code.** A change is applied by the process settings page's loading function (`Tab::load_config`). That code runs OrcaSlicer's settings clean-up rules (`ConfigManipulation.cpp`), and some of those rules open a blocking dialog or quietly rewrite another setting. Every key the assistant may change was checked against those rules so the preview can warn about them first. The printer page runs different code, and none of it has been checked. This is your item 3.
- **Where a value comes from is only proven for process settings.** A printer setting's value can come from the printer's base profile or the user's saved printer; the tools were not allowed to report that until it was proven.
- **The planned tools already include this.** In the guide's planned tool list, `settings_search`, `settings_get`, `settings_preview_patch` and `settings_apply_patch` are all listed as "extended to the same scopes and targets", with an optional `persistAs` to save the result as a named preset. That matches your items 1 and 2.

## One thing that affects your item 4

The printer conversation offers only one tool at a time on purpose. The guide says: "Home's printer panel runs its own conversation with exactly one tool per mode": `printer_identify` when adding a printer, and `printer_change` when changing one. It gives two reasons:

- A Change conversation that could also identify a printer "could clear the card of the printer it is about."
- The Change conversation is very small: about 552 input tokens per request.

Adding the four settings tools there reverses that decision, so it needs its own justification.

**Not checked:** the Entire session history. `entire search` failed with "no matching repositories found for [TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin]", so this repo is not mirrored there. Everything above comes from git history and `agent-docs`.

The recorded reason is only that process settings came first. Printer settings were postponed until someone did the same safety checking for them. No document says printer settings were risky or should stay off-limits.

The full reasoning, pieced together from the design doc that shipped with the tools (commit `77c0c6a3c4`, 2026-09-04):

1. **Process settings came first because a user's print questions land there.** Layer height, walls, infill and supports are what "make it stronger" or "print faster" change. I'm inferring this part; the doc never says why process settings were chosen.
2. **A change applied through a settings page can open a blocking dialog or quietly rewrite another setting.** The tools apply changes the same way the settings page does, so OrcaSlicer's clean-up rules run afterwards. To keep that from happening unseen, the design required checking every rule that each changeable setting could trigger. That checking had been done only for the process page's rules.
3. **No layer was offered before it was tested.** The design required every settings kind to be tested before the assistant could name it: printer, filament, plate, object and modifier alike. That rule doesn't single out printer settings.

That covers everything written down. The design doc treats "process only"

The agent’s critique is directionally useful, but it overcorrects in several places and—most importantly—evaluates the wrong deployment architecture. For JusPrin, an embedded, live OrcaSlicer integration is already the product decision; a headless CLI server is not an alternative we need to consider.

### Where the agent is right

- **Output size needs first-class design.** Large project and slice responses should support projections such as `summary`, `fields`, `limit`, `cursor`, and `changed_since_revision`. MCP’s `outputSchema` and `structuredContent` should define stable machine-readable results. Standard MCP pagination applies to protocol list operations; pagination inside an Orca-specific tool result must be designed by us. [MCP tools specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools)

- **Errors must be actionable.** A setting failure should return a stable error code plus structured details such as the canonical key, allowed values, valid scopes, conflicting settings, suggestions, and the current revision. Recoverable validation failures belong in tool results with `isError: true`; malformed MCP requests remain protocol errors.

- **Effective values need provenance.** `settings.get_values` cannot return only `0.2`. It needs something closer to:
  `effective_value`, `source`, `editable_scope`, `overridden_layers`, and `dependent_effects`. The agent is also right that a single `scope` enum does not capture Orca’s configuration behavior. However, its proposed hierarchy should not be assumed to be one universal linear inheritance chain; different settings support different owners and override mechanisms.

- **Concurrency and stale reads matter.** Live GUI edits require project-session identity and monotonic revisions. This is already central to JusPrin’s architecture and implementation: tool proposals carry a session and expected revision, and pending actions are invalidated when authoritative state changes. See [ToolExecution.hpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecution.hpp:3) and [ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:61).

- **Evaluation should drive the final surface.** Real tasks should test discovery, incorrect keys, conflicting settings, GUI edits between proposal and approval, cancellation, slicing, and undo behavior.

### Where it is overstated or wrong

| Agent claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Resources are mostly unsupported and should only be a bonus | The portability concern is valid, but “mostly unsupported” is an unsupported generalization. MCP deliberately makes resources **application-controlled**, and allows explicit selection, search, or automatic inclusion. The current protocol also supports caching and subscriptions. Because JusPrin controls its host, we can implement resource use deliberately. [MCP resources specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/resources) |
| Move all on-demand data behind getter tools | Too sweeping. Model-initiated searches should be tools, but large cacheable documents and reports remain good resources. A tool can return a concise result plus a resource link for the detailed report. Duplicating every resource as a getter tool creates another redundant API surface. |
| Workflow tools inherently put reasoning in the wrong place | Too categorical. Opaque opinionated mutations such as `optimize_for_strength` are questionable, but deterministic domain procedures such as generating a calibration object, arranging a plate, validating a change set, or starting a slice absolutely belong behind tools. The distinction is deterministic capability versus opaque discretionary policy—not “primitive versus workflow.” |
| Use one generic workflow tool with a workflow name | This solves tool-count arithmetic by weakening the schema. It can turn the tool into a hidden command bus with a growing enum and unrelated parameters. Group workflows only when they genuinely share inputs, outputs, approval behavior, and execution semantics. |
| Ten to twenty tools is the correct target | It is a useful initial budget, not a best-practice constant. The right count comes from schema-token measurements and tool-selection evals. Modern clients may also support deferred tool loading. |
| Dotted names may be rejected by MCP | Incorrect as an MCP claim. The current specification explicitly permits dots and even gives `admin.tools.list` as a valid example. Underscores may still be a sensible cross-provider portability convention, but that is a compatibility choice, not an MCP requirement. |
| Models know common Orca keys, so schema lookup can often be skipped | The conclusion is partly reasonable; the premise is unsafe. A separate lookup need not be mandatory, but every write must still be validated against the running Orca version. Training familiarity is not an API contract. |

### The central JusPrin-specific correction

The agent presents this as a decision between a headless CLI product and an embedded product. That decision is already made:

- Orca’s C++ model, canvases, slicer, and undo stack remain authoritative.
- The Agent UI is embedded in `wxWebView`.
- Future MCP support must use the existing typed workspace boundary.
- Operations must reuse Orca’s native command paths rather than simulate GUI input or create shadow state.

That is explicitly documented in [architecture.md](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/architecture.md:22) and [orca-integration-guide.md](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/orca-integration-guide.md:10).

The proper relationship is:

`MCP adapter → ToolExecutionCoordinator → IWorkspace → authoritative Orca owners`

MCP should be an external protocol adapter over that boundary, not the internal Orca integration abstraction and not a CLI wrapper.

### What the agent still misses

- **Approval and physical safety.** Setting mutations, deletion, export, calibration-profile updates, and sending a print require different approval policies. MCP annotations such as `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, and `idempotentHint` are useful, but they are only hints; JusPrin must enforce policy itself. MCP also recommends visible invocation and human confirmation. [MCP tools specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools)

- **Two-phase settings mutation.** A generic dynamic settings map is compact, but its JSON Schema cannot express every setting’s type and constraints. A safer shape is:
  1. Search/read authoritative setting metadata.
  2. Preview and validate a proposed patch.
  3. Show normalized values, conflicts, derived effects, and profile impact.
  4. Apply the approved patch against an expected revision.

- **Long-running operations.** Slicing, arrangement, repair, and calibration generation need progress, cancellation, completion, and stale-result semantics. They should not behave like synchronous getter calls.

- **Undo safety.** In a live application, `undo_last_operation` might undo a human edit made after the agent’s action. Every mutation should create one appropriate Orca snapshot and return the resulting revision/history position. Agent-triggered undo should require an expected revision/history token—or remain a direct human control. No shadow undo stack should be added.

Keep the original proposal’s “few verbs, settings as data” foundation. Incorporate the agent’s strong points about bounded outputs, structured errors, value provenance, stale revisions, and evals. Reject its headless-versus-embedded framing, its blanket demotion of resources and workflow tools, and its claim that dotted tool names violate MCP.

For JusPrin specifically, the most important design principle is not “tools versus resources.” It is:

> Every MCP operation must be a bounded, revision-aware, approval-aware projection of the authoritative live OrcaSlicer workspace contract.

Yes, with a few important changes. I would approve the first two ideas, but revise the MCP lifecycle and security details.

### 1. Shared tool registry: strongly agree

The hard-coded catalog in [OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp:62) should become one authoritative operation registry.

The registry should contain:

- Canonical tool name and title
- Semantic description
- Canonical input and output schemas
- Action class
- Execution behavior: immediate, approval-gated, or asynchronous
- Capability/version requirements
- Handler or coordinator dispatch identity

But “every tool serves both clients” should mean **one definition, filtered exposure**, not necessarily identical catalogs. The in-app agent and external MCP clients have different trust boundaries and capabilities. For example, external clients may receive a read-only subset unless explicitly authorized.

Also, adapters should not supply or decide the action class. The coordinator should look it up from the trusted registry. Otherwise an adapter bug could accidentally classify a mutation as read-only.

Because OpenAI strict schemas and MCP JSON Schema are not identical contracts, the registry should have protocol-specific serializers rather than assuming one JSON blob can always be copied verbatim.

### 2. Incremental workspace expansion: agree

This matches the project’s existing engineering discipline: narrow commands, authoritative Orca paths, fake contract tests, and real native-adapter tests.

I would refine the sequence slightly:

1. `settings_search` and `settings_get`
2. `settings_preview_patch`
3. `settings_apply_patch`
4. Asynchronous slicing and result inspection
5. Presets
6. Existing geometry commands such as transform and arrange
7. Export

Settings writes should not begin as a single direct “set arbitrary values” operation. The preview step should resolve effective values, validate scopes, show normalized before/after values, identify dependent changes, and bind the proposal to a workspace revision.

For slicing, the internal completion should indeed produce a workspace change. But that change should only be an invalidation/completion signal—not the result payload. Consumers should retrieve the authoritative slice result afterward, consistent with [the existing event guidance](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/orca-integration-guide.md:40).

### 3. MCP as a coordinator client: agree

This is the correct architecture:

`OpenAI adapter ─┐`  
`MCP adapter ────┼→ ToolExecutionCoordinator → IWorkspace → Orca owners`  
`future agents ──┘`

The transport thread must never touch Orca objects. It should marshal requests to the GUI thread, submit them through the coordinator, and receive structured completion asynchronously. That preserves the ownership rules in [architecture.md](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/architecture.md:47).

### 4. Transport security: mostly agree

For Streamable HTTP, loopback binding, authentication, and Origin validation are explicitly recommended or required by MCP. [The current transport specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/streamable-http) requires Origin validation, recommends binding local servers to `127.0.0.1`, and recommends authentication.

I would add:

- Bind numeric loopback addresses, not merely the `localhost` hostname.
- Validate `Host` as defense in depth alongside `Origin`.
- Reject oversized bodies and rate-limit requests.
- Keep MCP disabled by default with a visible status and immediate kill switch.
- Never accept arbitrary local paths without explicit access policy.
- Store bearer secrets in OS-protected credentials, never logs or URLs.

“Per-session token” needs clarification. MCP 2026-07-28 removed protocol-level sessions. Use either:

- A per-process random bearer secret, or
- A persistent, revocable paired-client credential.

Do not confuse either with JusPrin’s `project session ID`, which exists to invalidate stale object IDs.

### 5. Do not use progress notifications as the lifecycle

This is the main correction.

MCP progress notifications are optional, requested by the client, tied to one active request, and require monotonically increasing progress. They can supplement execution with messages such as “waiting for local approval” or “slicing layer data,” but they should not be the authoritative carrier for `pending → awaiting approval → running → completed`.

For external clients:

- Immediate reads return normally.
- Approval-gated actions return an explicit `action_id`, or use MCP input-required semantics if approval is being collected by the client.
- Long-running slicing uses an explicit job/activity handle.
- If the client advertises the MCP Tasks extension, map the activity to a task.
- Otherwise provide a small status/cancel interface.
- Progress notifications remain optional decoration.

The 2026 protocol deliberately uses explicit handles for state across calls and provides the Tasks extension for long-running work. [MCP 2026-07-28 changes](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/)

JusPrin’s existing `ToolActivity` already supplies most of the correct internal state model: action ID, session, expected revision, approval requirement, progress, structured result, cancellation, and terminal states. See [ToolExecution.hpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecution.hpp:16).

### 6. “Reuse nothing from the Orca PR”: too absolute

I agree that PR #12667 should not become the foundation. It targets the older 2025-03-26 session-based protocol and lacks the security and coordinator architecture JusPrin requires.

But “reuse nothing” discards useful evidence. The PR already contains a Boost ASIO transport, tool-schema registry, GUI-thread dispatch experience, Catch2 tests, and documented failures involving modal dialogs, slice status, screenshots, and object deletion. [OrcaSlicer PR #12667](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer/pull/12667)

The right stance is:

> Do not transplant its architecture or handlers. Inspect its implementation, failures, and tests; reuse only isolated protocol or test ideas that fit JusPrin’s boundary and current MCP version.

So overall: **yes to the shared registry, incremental workspace commands, and MCP-over-coordinator architecture; no to treating progress as the lifecycle, exposing every tool identically, or ignoring all evidence from the existing PR.**

Consumers should retrieve the authoritative slice result afterward, consistent with [the existing event guidance](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/orca-integration-guide.md:40).

### 3. MCP as a coordinator client: agree

This is the correct architecture:

`OpenAI adapter ─┐`  
`MCP adapter ────┼→ ToolExecutionCoordinator → IWorkspace → Orca owners`  
`future agents ──┘`

The transport thread must never touch Orca objects. It should marshal requests to the GUI thread, submit them through the coordinator, and receive structured completion asynchronously. That preserves the ownership rules in [architecture.md](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/architecture.md:47).

### 4. Transport security: mostly agree

For Streamable HTTP, loopback binding, authentication, and Origin validation are explicitly recommended or required by MCP. [The current transport specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/transports/streamable-http) requires Origin validation, recommends binding local servers to `127.0.0.1`, and recommends authentication.

I would add:

- Bind numeric loopback addresses, not merely the `localhost` hostname.
- Validate `Host` as defense in depth alongside `Origin`.
- Reject oversized bodies and rate-limit requests.
- Keep MCP disabled by default with a visible status and immediate kill switch.
- Never accept arbitrary local paths without explicit access policy.
- Store bearer secrets in OS-protected credentials, never logs or URLs.

“Per-session token” needs clarification. MCP 2026-07-28 removed protocol-level sessions. Use either:

- A per-process random bearer secret, or
- A persistent, revocable paired-client credential.

Do not confuse either with JusPrin’s `project session ID`, which exists to invalidate stale object IDs.

### 5. Do not use progress notifications as the lifecycle

This is the main correction.

MCP progress notifications are optional, requested by the client, tied to one active request, and require monotonically increasing progress. They can supplement execution with messages such as “waiting for local approval” or “slicing layer data,” but they should not be the authoritative carrier for `pending → awaiting approval → running → completed`.

For external clients:

- Immediate reads return normally.
- Approval-gated actions return an explicit `action_id`, or use MCP input-required semantics if approval is being collected by the client.
- Long-running slicing uses an explicit job/activity handle.
- If the client advertises the MCP Tasks extension, map the activity to a task.
- Otherwise provide a small status/cancel interface.
- Progress notifications remain optional decoration.

The 2026 protocol deliberately uses explicit handles for state across calls and provides the Tasks extension for long-running work. [MCP 2026-07-28 changes](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/)

JusPrin’s existing `ToolActivity` already supplies most of the correct internal state model: action ID, session, expected revision, approval requirement, progress, structured result, cancellation, and terminal states. See [ToolExecution.hpp](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecution.hpp:16).

### 6. “Reuse nothing from the Orca PR”: too absolute

I agree that PR #12667 should not become the foundation. It targets the older 2025-03-26 session-based protocol and lacks the security and coordinator architecture JusPrin requires.

But “reuse nothing” discards useful evidence. The PR already contains a Boost ASIO transport, tool-schema registry, GUI-thread dispatch experience, Catch2 tests, and documented failures involving modal dialogs, slice status, screenshots, and object deletion. [OrcaSlicer PR #12667](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer/pull/12667)

The right stance is:

> Do not transplant its architecture or handlers. Inspect its implementation, failures, and tests; reuse only isolated protocol or test ideas that fit JusPrin’s boundary and current MCP version.

So overall: **yes to the shared registry, incremental workspace commands, and MCP-over-coordinator architecture; no to treating progress as the lifecycle, exposing every tool identically, or ignoring all evidence from the existing PR.**

content.text:
The rule came out of a design review on 2026-09-02/03, before any settings tool existed. A proposed design gave the settings tool a single `scope` field covering `project | plate | object | filament | printer | process`. A second agent objected that one field can't describe how a value's origin works in OrcaSlicer: each kind of setting has its own owner and its own way of being overridden. The fix was to ship process settings only and add the other kinds one at a time. Nobody argued that printer settings should stay off-limits.

## What happened, in order

**1. 2026-09-03, first critique.** You asked an agent to critique a proposed OrcaSlicer MCP design (MCP is the protocol external AI tools use to call JusPrin). You pasted that critique into a Codex session (`~/.codex/sessions/2026/09/02/rollout-2026-09-02T18-09-50-…jsonl`) and asked Codex to critique it in turn. The proposal's settings tool was one call with `"scope": "project | plate | object | filament | printer | process"`. The critique you pasted called this the hardest problem in the design:

> The settings inheritance model. This is the hardest real design problem for OrcaSlicer and the document waves it away with a `scope` enum. Orca settings layer: printer/filament/process preset → project override → per-plate → per-object modifier. An agent will constantly need "what is the effective value here and which layer set it." If `get_values` doesn't answer that, the agent will make wrong edits at the wrong layer.

**2. Codex agreed, with one correction** (01:14 UTC):

> The agent is also right that a single `scope` enum does not capture Orca's configuration behavior. However, its proposed hierarchy should not be assumed to be one universal linear inheritance chain; different settings support different owners and override mechanisms.

It also said every value the tools return must say which layer it came from.

**3. The first implementation doc turned that into a rule** (01:33 UTC, `mcp-v1-implementation-handoff.md`, section "Settings scope in v1", never committed):

> Support only the active FFF **process** preset's edited configuration. Do not expose a generic `scope` field that implies support for printer, filament, plate, object, or modifier layers. Add those scopes later as separate tested capabilities…
>
> The v1 source model is intentionally narrow. Do not claim to report full printer/filament/project/object inheritance until the workspace contract can prove it.

The same session had already set the build order: settings search and read first, then preview, then apply, then slicing, presets, transforms, arrange and export.

**4. The rule was then copied forward.** On 2026-09-04, Claude session `12b61c09…` wrote `mcp-settings-tools-handoff.md` from that doc. It labelled the rule "Decisions already made… restated only so nobody reopens them," and added "until each is a separately tested capability." Commit `62c0606a09` (2026-09-08) moved it into [mcp-tool-extension-guide.md](agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md) as standing decision 2. Object overrides were later added through `target` in `c35dcfcd20`.

## What this means for printer settings

The objection was never to printer settings. It was to a `scope` field that promised every layer before the tools could correctly report where a value came from. Adding `scope: printer` fits the original intent, as long as reads correctly say whether a printer value comes from the system profile or the user's saved printer.

The Entire session index isn't available for this repo, so I found this by searching the raw session logs under `~/.codex/sessions` and `~/.claude/projects`.
